strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and important gap: unsupervised Bayesian model selection and misspecification diagnosis in imaging when only a single noisy measurement is available and priors are implicit (e.g., diffusion, plug-and-play). Existing alternatives (marginal likelihood via nested sampling, harmonic mean estimators, empirical Bayes residuals) are either computationally prohibitive or unreliable, motivating the approach.

The core idea—combining Bayesian cross-validation with data fission/measurement splitting—is elegant, well-motivated, and presented clearly. The connection to the marginal likelihood as a limiting case (α→0, likelihood rule) provides a principled framing: the method is a computationally tractable relaxation of the gold standard.

The proposed scoring rules are sensible and complementary: a likelihood-based rule (Eq. 5/8) suited to likelihood misspecification and a posterior-based rule with perceptual embeddings (Eq. 6/9) that is sensitive to prior/OOD misspecification. The theoretical explanation of why Φ2 detects OOD (noise imbalance between y+ and y- creates perceptual discrepancy in hallucinated samples) is convincing and illustrated in Figures 7-10.

Experiments are reasonably broad: a controlled Gaussian toy study analyzing the role of α, K, and dimensionality; kernel model selection where the method substantially outperforms Bayesian/empirical-Bayes residual baselines (86.7% single-shot, 100% few-shot vs. 40-60%); OOD detection on natural images and MRI across blur levels, acceleration factors, and Gaussian/Poisson noise; and Type I error/power tables that roughly respect the nominal 5% level.

Reproducibility is addressed (public code, implementation details in the appendix), and the supplementary material is honest about limitations: slow convergence of the Monte Carlo estimator and growing error with dimension (Figs. 11-13), failure cases of Φ2 at extreme blur or poor α choices (Figs. 15-16), and sensitivity of Φ2 to the choice of perceptual embedding (discussed for MRI).
weaknesses: Theoretical support is thin. There are no formal results on the bias/variance of the fission-based CV estimator, its consistency as K,N grow, or how detection/selection power behaves in high dimensions. The error analysis is confined to a 1D-prior Gaussian toy model where error is shown to grow substantially with dimension m (Fig. 12)—precisely the regime of interest for imaging—so the practical high-dimensional behavior remains empirically observed rather than understood.

The 'fully unsupervised from a single measurement' claim is weakened in the misspecification-testing experiments: the statistical test requires a reference ID dataset (30-60 images) to calibrate the 95th-percentile threshold of Φ2. Model selection against a known reference model is one thing; calibrated OOD testing without any reference data is not demonstrated.

The hyperparameter α materially affects results (Figs. 1, 14, 15 show large changes in detection power and error rates across α), but there is no principled procedure for choosing it; different experiments use α = 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 apparently by hand. A methodology that requires case-by-case tuning of a central knob limits ease of adoption.

Baseline comparisons are limited. The only quantitative comparison is against the residual method [55] in the kernel-selection experiment; for OOD detection, the recent unsupervised diffusion-based OOD method [48]—which the paper itself cites—is not compared against, making it hard to judge the incremental value of the new machinery for that task.

The posterior-based rule Φ2 is heuristic rather than a proper scoring rule, and its behavior depends strongly on the embedding (LPIPS fails on some cases; DINOv2 recovers 100% accuracy on brain images). The framework's performance is thus partly contingent on embedding choices that are not well characterized, and the paper's failure modes (e.g., Φ2 favoring a hallucinating model in Fig. 20a) are acknowledged but not resolved.

Some evaluations rest on very small samples (e.g., 15 selection experiments in Table 5; 30 test images in Table 2), so accuracy/power estimates carry substantial uncertainty; no confidence intervals or repeated trials are reported for the main tables.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underserved problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification testing for Bayesian imaging inverse problems from a single noisy measurement, which is a real bottleneck for deploying data-driven priors in scientific imaging.

The core idea of combining data fission (measurement splitting by noise injection) with Bayesian cross-validation is elegant and natural, and the connection to posterior predictive checks and the marginal likelihood (Section 3.3, Eqs. 10-11) is clearly articulated, positioning the method as a computationally tractable relaxation of evidence computation.

The methodology is sampler-agnostic and demonstrated with both plug-and-play Langevin (SK-ROCK) and diffusion-based (DiffPIR) samplers, plus extensions to Poisson noise, supporting the generality claim.

The supplementary material is thorough: analytical derivations for the Gaussian case, ablations over alpha and K, negative-result discussions (e.g., failure cases in Fig. 16, effect of blur strength on detection power), and implementation details.
Empirical results are respectable: 86.7% single-shot kernel selection accuracy versus 40-60% for the residual-based baselines, and reasonable Type I error/power calibration in the OOD experiments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility statement is broken: the code URL, model links, and dataset links are literally blank in the manuscript ('available at' followed by nothing). For a paper whose main claims are entirely empirical, this is a serious deficiency for verification at review time.

No theoretical analysis of the proposed estimators. The paper provides no bias/variance analysis of Phi-hat for the actual estimators used (Eqs. 8-9), only an empirical Gaussian toy study. Notably, Phi1 averages log-likelihoods while the logarithmic score applies log to an average; the Jensen gap between these is acknowledged but never quantified, and its magnitude relative to model discrimination gaps in high dimensions (Fig. 12 shows relative error growing with m) is not established.

The mechanism underlying the posterior-based rule Phi2 is presented only heuristically ('noise imbalance creates a noticeable perceptual discrepancy'). It is unclear whether Phi2 measures model misspecification or is confounded by image content: LPIPS-embedding distances between posterior samples may simply track whether the prior can represent the image, which overlaps with, but is not identical to, prior misspecification. The MRI results (Phi2 underperforming Phi1 on knee images, requiring a switch to DINOv2 embeddings to reach 100%) underscore that the method's success depends on embedding choices that are not principled.

Baselines are thin. The only quantitative comparisons are against the Bayesian/empirical-Bayesian residual methods of [55] on a 3-image kernel-selection task with 5 candidate kernels. No comparison against the diffusion-based unsupervised OOD method cited as [48], which is the closest related work; the paper claims novelty ('no existing methods can diagnose OOD based on a single measurement') without empirically substantiating the advantage over that prior work.

Several methodological choices are ad hoc: alpha is hand-tuned per experiment (0.5, 0.1, 0.25 with a different rationale in each), the statistical test is a raw 95th-percentile threshold on a reference dataset, and no guidance is given on how to set K, N, or alpha in a new application. The reported excellent results thus partly reflect careful per-experiment tuning that practitioners cannot easily replicate.

Experimental scope is narrow relative to the framing: only Gaussian/Poisson deblurring and single-coil MRI, with small test sets (e.g., 15 single-shot selection trials, 30-90 test images for OOD). The claimed generality ('compatible with any Bayesian imaging sampler', 'general methodology') is not stress-tested on, e.g., severely ill-posed or nonlinear operators where the likelihood-based rule is acknowledged to have poor discrimination.

There is a tension in the story: the paper notes that alpha -> 0 recovers the marginal likelihood (the gold standard) but that this limit requires more Monte Carlo samples, and Fig. 1 shows discrimination degrading as alpha grows. Since the practical setting used for diffusion experiments is alpha = 0.1-0.25 with K = 4-10 noise realizations and N = 10-20 posterior samples per realization (explicitly under-converged per Fig. 18), the link between the framework's motivating theory and the operating regime actually used is weak, and it is not shown whether a simpler alternative (e.g., direct sample-based prior/likelihood sanity checks) would do comparably.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification testing in Bayesian imaging using only a single noisy measurement, which is genuinely unsolved for modern learned priors (diffusion, plug-and-play).

The combination of data fission / measurement splitting (Leiner et al. 2025; Pang et al. 2021; Monroy et al. 2025) with Bayesian cross-validation is a novel and natural idea, and the paper nicely positions it as a relaxation of the marginal likelihood (recovered as alpha -> 0), giving conceptual grounding.
The methodology is sampler-agnostic and demonstrated with two very different samplers (SK-ROCK plug-and-play Langevin and DiffPIR diffusion), increasing credibility of the generality claim.

Careful empirical framing of misspecification detection as a statistical test with Type I error and power (Tabs. 2, 3, 8), including a Poisson-noise extension showing the exponential-family generality (SM C.2).

Thorough supporting analysis: exact Gaussian analytic derivation (SM A), bias-reduction via averaging over K noise realizations (Fig. 2), sensitivity to alpha (Figs. 14-15), and honest discussion of failure modes (e.g., Fig. 16, knee-model under-training).
Code is stated to be publicly available and implementation details (hyperparameters, padding handling, compute budget) are documented, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: No theoretical guarantees for the proposed estimators: bias/variance behavior, consistency, or error rates of Phi_1 and Phi_2 are only studied empirically and in the toy Gaussian case; the paper is essentially a methodology + experiments contribution.

The 'fully unsupervised, single measurement' claim is weakened in the OOD experiments: the test threshold is calibrated at the 95th percentile of the statistic over a reference ID dataset (60 FFHQ images, 50 brain scans), so a labeled in-distribution reference set is still required for detection.

Baseline coverage is thin: the only comparison is the residual-based method of Vidal et al. [55]; the closest related unsupervised diffusion OOD method [48] (Shoushtari et al.) is cited but not compared against, making it hard to judge the empirical state of the art.

Some experiments are small-scale: kernel selection uses only 3 test images (15 single-shot trials), and reference/test sets are 50-60 images, so accuracy figures like 86.7% carry substantial uncertainty.

Effectiveness of the posterior-based rule Phi_2 depends heavily on the embedding choice (LPIPS fails on MRI; DinoV2 fixes it, SM C.3) and on the splitting parameter alpha, both of which are largely hand-tuned hyperparameters without principled selection guidance.

Computational cost is claimed to be low, but the method requires K noise realizations with N posterior samples each from two posteriors; a systematic cost comparison against nested sampling or the marginal likelihood baselines is not provided.

Presentation issues: duplicated references ([28]/[29] and [41]/[42] are identical), missing URLs in the code/reproducibility footnotes, and minor typos (e.g., 'the the' in Tab. 1 caption, stray parenthesis in Eq. (4)).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important gap: unsupervised model selection and misspecification diagnosis for Bayesian imaging with implicit (ML-learned) priors, where only a single noisy measurement is available and marginal-likelihood/evidence methods are computationally intractable.

The core methodology is a sensible and, to my knowledge, novel combination of data fission (Leiner et al. 2025; Pang et al. 2021; Monroy et al. 2025) with partial predictive (Bayesian cross-validation) evaluation, made compatible with general Bayesian samplers (plug-and-play Langevin, DiffPIR), which increases its practical reach.

There is a meaningful theoretical component: Proposition 1 (with a careful dominated-convergence proof in the SM) shows the framework recovers the marginal likelihood as the splitting parameter α → 0, positioning the method as a computationally tractable relaxation of Bayesian evidence; the extensive Gaussian case study (analytical derivations in SM Section C) quantifies the bias/variance and accuracy/cost trade-offs of the split.

The experimental evaluation is broad and reasonably convincing: likelihood-based blur-kernel selection (86.7% single-shot accuracy, clearly beating residual-based baselines of Vidal et al. 2021), prior selection and OOD detection with Type I error/power analysis on natural images and MRI, a comparison against proximal nested sampling for log-evidence (rankings agree), ablations over embeddings (LPIPS, DINOv2, CLIP, DreamSim), extension to Poisson noise, and robustness to sampler degradation.

Reproducibility is good: code is released, implementation details, run times, and hyperparameter choices are documented, and the appendix honestly discusses failure cases (e.g., Φ̂² misclassification under strong blur, catastrophic sampler failure at low iteration counts) without overselling.
weaknesses: No general accuracy guarantees: the estimator error analysis is essentially confined to the linear-Gaussian toy case; for the diffusion-prior experiments the quality of Φ̂¹ and Φ̂² depends entirely on (uncontrolled) posterior sampling error, and there is no bound or diagnostic for the induced bias in non-Gaussian settings.

The posterior-based rule Φ̂², arguably the paper's main practical contribution for prior probing and OOD detection, is fairly heuristic: it hinges on a perceptual embedding choice, the ablation shows results vary substantially across embeddings (DreamSim fails badly, CLIP is unstable), and no principled guidance is given for choosing the embedding or the α/threshold configuration, which is set per experiment (α = 0.1 vs 0.25/0.5 across experiments).

Baseline coverage is limited: comparisons are mainly against the Bayesian/empirical-Bayes residual methods of Vidal et al. (2021) and ProxNest evidence estimation; the closely related unsupervised diffusion-based OOD method of Shoushtari et al. (2025) is cited and its priors are even reused, but is not compared against empirically.

Statistical evaluation uses small test sets (e.g., 15–60 ID images, 50-image OOD sets), so reported Type I error rates quantized at ~6.7% carry high variance; more systematic repetition or larger sets would strengthen the claims of 'excellent' detection accuracy.

The α → 0 limit that connects the method to the marginal likelihood is exactly the regime that is computationally prohibitive (as the Gaussian analysis itself shows), so in practice the method is an uncontrolled approximation of a gold standard; the paper frames this honestly but the gap in realistic regimes is only assessed empirically.

Significance is somewhat specialized: the contribution is most relevant to the computational imaging/Bayesian imaging community, and the method still requires many posterior samples (e.g., 210+ draws per image at ~1.5–8.6 s each), which may limit adoption despite being cheaper than nested sampling.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification diagnosis for Bayesian imaging from a single noisy measurement, which is highly relevant given the prevalence of implicit deep-learning priors (diffusion, plug-and-play) where marginal likelihood computation is intractable.

The combination of data fission / recorrupted-to-recorrupted splitting (Pang et al., 2021; Leiner et al., 2025; Monroy et al., 2025) with partial-posterior predictive evaluation is a sensible and clean construction, and Proposition 1 (with a correct dominated-convergence proof) nicely situates the estimator as a relaxation of the marginal likelihood recovered as α → 0.

Empirical evaluation is comparatively thorough: an analytically tractable Gaussian case with derived formulas and convergence/dimension/α studies (Figs. 2-3, 12-16), kernel-family selection (86.7% single-shot accuracy vs. 40-60% for residual baselines), OOD detection on natural images and MRI with Type I error/power reporting, a comparison against proximal nested sampling (Appendix B, rankings matching logZ), embedding ablations (LPIPS/DINOv2/CLIP/Dreamsim), Poisson-noise extension, and robustness to sampler degradation.
The method is sampler-agnostic in principle (demonstrated with SK-ROCK PnP and DiffPIR), and computational overhead is honestly quantified (Table 4, Appendix A.2).
weaknesses: The 'fully unsupervised, single measurement' framing is undermined in the misspecification-testing setting: the OOD tests require a reference in-distribution dataset (50-60 images) to calibrate the 95th-percentile threshold. The methodology therefore relies on auxiliary calibration data whose availability contradicts, in part, the motivating claim that only one measurement is available; this tension is not acknowledged as a limitation.

The posterior-based rule Φ2y has weak statistical foundations. Its effectiveness is explained qualitatively ('noise imbalance between y+ and y− creates a perceptual discrepancy'), not by any formal argument that the statistic targets prior misspecification rather than sampler artifacts, embedding bias (LPIPS trained on natural images performs poorly on MRI, Sec. E.6), or α-dependent posterior spread. The test's validity under the null is empirical only, and Type I error control degrades with α (Fig. 18) and with small reference sets.

Theoretical support is thin relative to the claims: only the α → 0 limit is proven, recovering the marginal likelihood — precisely the computationally intractable quantity the paper aims to avoid. No bias/variance bounds or discrimination-power analysis is provided for the finite-α estimators actually used, and the α trade-off is handled purely empirically.

Methodological novelty is incremental: data fission splitting, cross-validation logic, and predictive scoring rules are each established; the contribution is their assembly in the imaging setting, plus two scoring-rule instantiations.

Evaluation is limited to deblurring and single-coil MRI at 256×256, with small test sets (15-90 images) and only two misspecified-prior comparisons in the main experiments (FFHQ vs. AFHQ; brain vs. knee). No comparison against the recent single-measurement-relevant OOD method of Shoushtari et al. (2025) in the main experiments, and the kernel-selection experiment uses a fixed, hand-tuned regularization parameter (λ=110) that itself introduces prior misspecification acknowledged by the authors.

The method requires knowing the noise model exactly to perform the split (Gaussian covariance Σ, Poisson intensity γ); robustness to misspecification of the noise model — a natural failure mode — is not studied.

Reproducibility is compromised: the 'Software and Data' section states the code is 'available at' with no URL given, and model/download links are likewise blank, so the work cannot currently be reproduced or verified.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification diagnosis for Bayesian imaging with only a single noisy measurement is an important and underexplored gap, especially for data-driven (diffusion, plug-and-play) priors where marginal likelihood methods fail.

The proposed approach is a clean and sensible combination of Bayesian cross-validation (partial predictive summaries) with data fission/measurement splitting by noise injection, and is agnostic to the sampler class (validated with SK-ROCK PnP and DiffPIR, plus a Poisson variant).

A valuable theoretical anchor: Proposition 1 shows the estimator recovers the marginal likelihood as α → 0, positioning the method as a computationally efficient relaxation of the Bayes factor; this is supported by an extensive and careful Gaussian toy analysis (analytical derivations in Appendix C, error-vs-α, error-vs-dimension, convergence of the approximate Bayes factor).

Two well-differentiated scoring rules (likelihood-based Φ1 for likelihood misspecification, posterior/perceptual Φ2 for prior/OOD diagnosis), with an embedding ablation (LPIPS, DINOv2, CLIP, Dreamsim) that honestly reports where each fails (e.g., CLIP), rather than cherry-picking.

Empirically strong and reasonably thorough evaluation: kernel model selection from a single measurement (86.7% vs 40–60% for Bayesian residual baselines), OOD detection with calibrated Type I error near 5% and high power on FFHQ/CelebA/LSUN/Met-Faces and FastMRI brain-vs-knee, ranking agreement with ProxNest log-evidence, robustness-to-sampler-degradation and α-sensitivity ablations, and computational cost reporting.

Good reproducibility posture: pseudo-code, implementation details (GPU, sampling budgets), and code/data availability; limitations such as sampler breakdown and failure cases (Fig. 19, Sec. E.5) are openly discussed.
weaknesses: The theory is comparatively light relative to the empirical content: the only formal result is the α → 0 limit (Proposition 1); there is no analysis of the estimator's bias/variance for finite α beyond the Gaussian toy case, nor any calibration theory for the Φ2-based test (the 5% threshold is purely empirical on a reference dataset).

The behavior of the posterior-based rule Φ2 rests largely on an informal mechanism (noise imbalance between y+ and y− under OOD inducing perceptual discrepancy), which is convincing empirically but is a heuristic argument; the method's power in mild-OOD regimes degrades noticeably (60–73% at σκ = 5), and failure cases exist.

The methodology assumes the noise model, noise level, and an admissible splitting scheme are known/available (Gaussian and Poisson covered; other exponential-family cases cited but not derived/tested); misspecification of the noise model itself is not addressed, which is a real limitation for the stated goal of misspecification testing.

Experimental scope is limited to deblurring, denoising, and single-coil MRI with synthetic degradations; baselines are few (Bayesian residuals and ProxNest) and there is no direct comparison to the diffusion-specific OOD method of Shoushtari et al. (2025) on the same benchmarks.

Practical hyperparameter choices (α, K, N, L) appear somewhat dataset-dependent (α = 0.1 vs 0.25 vs 0.5 across experiments) without a principled selection procedure, which may limit out-of-the-box applicability.

Minor presentation issues: some equations/notation carry typos and inconsistencies (e.g., definitions of f+_α/f−_α across Eq. (3) and Appendix C/E, α used both as split ratio and sampling parameter), and the kernel-selection tables show near-tie values that make single-shot accuracy sensitive to Monte Carlo budget.
